claim.statement: As of 2 May 2026, fresh Persian evidence still points to containment rather than public rollback: ministry-linked statements deny that the government or Communications Ministry presented or licensed Internet Pro and blame operator violations, while the active policy architecture remains a security/SNSC-mediated exception channel for business, production, industry, and commerce users under authentication and security conditions.
claim.subject: official pressure over Internet Pro
claim.object: a security-mediated selective-access channel while disowning implementation abuse

evidence.summary: The re-crawled Bank Eghtesad/Jamaran/KhabarOnline source says international-internet scope and limits sit with security bodies/SNSC, the three operators are obligated to implement Internet Pro, and access is being expanded to authenticated business/production/industry/commerce units.

Iran International quotes Mohammad-Hafez Hokmi saying Internet Pro was not presented by the government, some operators implemented it for some businesses, violations occurred, and government policy rejects tiered internet.
The existing EghtesadOnline/ISNA source records the later Ministry-adviser denial that the Ministry issued no Internet Pro license and frames the problem as violations/bad implementation.
The v40 xPool sample after May 1 contains ordinary-user cutoff/restoration anger and ministry-denial discourse, but no source-near public restoration directive or measurable rollback.
The v40 notes compare the official denial layer with SNSC/security and operator implementation evidence.

information_depth.rationale: The claim is an inference across official/near-official reporting, an independent ministry-denial report, existing KNB rows, and a fresh xPool discourse check.

assessment.uncertainty: A formal regulator order canceling packages, an SNSC rollback text, operator notices, or network measurements showing ordinary public restoration would change this assessment.

claim.statement: April 2026 reporting makes Internet Pro operationally concrete rather than hypothetical: access is mediated through company letters, user lists, SIM/national-ID data, committee or operator review, and role-specific permissions; reported prices cluster around roughly 1.98m to 2.176m toman plus tax for 50GB/year, with one RighTel example capped at 2GB/day so daily 2GB use would imply about 14 repurchases and roughly 32m toman/year versus 383k toman for an ordinary 50GB package.
claim.subject: Internet Pro implementation
claim.object: public access into a priced, authenticated, role-differentiated entitlement

evidence.summary: AbanDaily reports RighTel's 2.176m toman pre-tax quote, 50GB/year with 2GB/day cap, no proof that listed users are employees, MCI around 2.04m toman, and the 32m/year implication for daily 2GB use.

Farnet reports official-letter and Excel-list mechanics, committee review under SNSC direction involving the Communications Ministry and National Cyberspace Center, 1.98m toman plus 10% VAT pricing, regulator non-involvement in tariff-setting, and access that varies by role/service.
The existing Iran International source had already described organizational applications, selected employees, undertakings, higher prices, and partial access rather than public restoration.
The v40 notes separate operator-pricing mechanics from the official denial layer.

information_depth.rationale: The details are specific and cross-source consistent, but still largely media-reported rather than a full regulator tariff file or official operator contract.

assessment.uncertainty: Precise package availability and pricing may vary by operator, role, and later enforcement; official tariff files and operator notices are still needed.

claim.statement: The v40 xPool sample after May 1 emitted 62 items (61 usable text rows) and showed continuing public anger rather than a restoration cluster: 40 posts mentioned Internet Pro, 7 tiered internet, 7 white-SIM/white-line language, 10 ministry/adviser denial language, 4 operator language, and 41 cutoff/restoration terms; manual review found 62-63-day cutoff complaints, refusal-to-legitimize discourse, ministry denials, and black-market activation claims, but no source-near public restoration directive.
claim.subject: v40 xPool Internet Pro sample
claim.object: continued blackout/tiered-access anger without a public restoration cluster

evidence.summary: The saved result has 62 emitted items after 10 pages; jq/manual counts found the term distribution and no source-near rollback or restoration directive.
The source notes record the xPool query, counts, saved raw paths, and manual-read summary.

information_depth.rationale: The result is a bounded X sample useful for discourse topology and negative evidence, not a representative measurement of all users or network state.

assessment.uncertainty: The sample was latest-search and term-constrained; restoration could be occurring outside the sampled terms or through network changes not discussed on X.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v40 - Internet Pro pressure forces denials, not restoration
synthesis.summary: The fortieth pass asks whether Internet Pro backlash has produced rollback for ordinary users. The answer is still no. Pressure is real: professional refusals, the Tehran E-Commerce Association, Article 90/Judiciary language, and fresh X discourse make tiered internet politically toxic. But the system response is responsibility-splitting, not public restoration. Security/SNSC bodies remain the authority for international-internet scope; operators implement and monetize access; the Communications Ministry says the label was not its plan and blames implementation violations; Parliament/judiciary language targets discrimination and profiteering. New operator evidence makes the model concrete: company letters, user lists, SIM/national-ID data, committee review, role-differentiated access, 1.98m-2.176m toman plus tax for 50GB/year, and a RighTel path that can imply roughly 32m toman/year for daily 2GB use. The v40 xPool sample reinforces the negative evidence: people are still talking about 62-63 days of cutoff, white SIMs, Internet Pro, black-market activation, and refusal to legitimize tiered access, not a public restoration directive. Net: the crack is legitimacy and administrative blame-shifting inside digital control; ordinary users remain behind filtering/cutoff while exceptions are authenticated, priced, and narrowed as crisis service.
synthesis.limitations: This pass is strong on public-source policy mechanics and discourse topology, but still lacks an official SNSC text, regulator tariff file, operator contract notice, allocation-list disclosure, or direct network measurements. A future formal cancellation/restoration directive or measured public restoration would change the read.

information_depth.rationale: The synthesis combines existing KNB Internet Pro rows, fresh direct crawls, a completed xPool sample, and explicit source-hygiene constraints.

operations.rationale: The claim directly answers the rollback-versus-containment question with fresh official-denial and SNSC/security-channel evidence.
The operator pricing and authentication mechanics explain what is being preserved when officials deny or narrow the Internet Pro label.
Internet Pro pricing and black-market activation are part of the wider pattern of crisis rents and information-control markets.
The social sample supplies negative evidence: backlash and denial discourse persisted, while public restoration did not surface in the sampled stream.
The sample shows the refusal coalition remains visible but did not newly break the tiered-access model in the sampled period.
